prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated in a magic-wavelength trap, and its realization at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep B024 as my single preferred part, and after round 1 I hold it for reasons that do not depend on the count of first places. The invention is one identifiable idea: a state-insensitive optical lattice in which the differential light shift of the clock transition vanishes, so that many atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil shifts. The realization is quantitative and has been checked by the only test a clock must pass, comparison between independent devices, with systematic uncertainty near 10^-18 reproduced in several laboratories and species. Ye's many-body, spin-polarized fermion clock work shows that the credit for the second name is physics and not only engineering performance. The consequences (limits on drifting constants, relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, the roadmap to a redefinition of the second) all follow from the result and are not conditions for it. I answer the chair's question on the 2005 and 2012 prizes this way: the comb is the ruler and single-ion control is a different object, whereas the lattice clock is a new regime of many neutral atoms with a stability that a single ion cannot reach in the same averaging time. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly so that this distinction is on the page. On the redefinition of the second, I now regard it as an administrative consummation and not as a prerequisite; the prize rewards the demonstrated performance, as Lindroth argued.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. A skeptic can still read B024 as the third prize in one lineage after 2005 and 2012, and a metrology prize can be read as an instrument achievement and not a discovery. Credit at the edges is not airtight: Lemonde, Hollberg, Sterr, Ludlow, Hinkley and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, and the ion-clock leaders, contributed to the ecosystem, and Ye's role could be described either as co-invention or as realization to record accuracy. I cannot resolve that chronology from the supplied record, which is why my citation says invention of the lattice clock and its realization and does not claim co-invention. B003 has a stronger claim to opening a new field of matter, and if the committee weights discovery of new phases above measurement precision, it is the serious competitor. My own weighing of B003 is held back by two things round 1 did not remove: the unsettled pairing mechanism and the omission of the first experimental author within the three-name limit.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B003 first as a discovery in nature of a state of matter nobody expected, argues that the clock is a refinement of a measurement we already knew how to make, and says B024 would be the safe and defensible alternative that he would not oppose.
responses.response: This is the sharpest statement of the real disagreement, and I concede part of it: B003 has more surprise content. I do not accept that the clock only sharpens an existing measurement. A lattice clock is a different physical system, many neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength trap, and it opened regimes that did not exist before, such as comparing clocks on millimetre height differences through the gravitational redshift and a many-body systematic budget. I also take your precedent on high-temperature superconductors seriously, and it persuades me that an unsettled pairing mechanism should not by itself block B003; I would write that citation on flat bands and correlated states only, as you propose. My remaining difficulty is the credit. Your own point that Cao and the early experimental leaders sit outside a three-name limit is a defect I cannot see how to repair, whereas for B024 I can defend two names. So I keep B024 first, but I now regard your B003 as a legitimate final choice and not merely a polite alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B024 only seventh because the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes create overlap and the citation must say precisely what is new, and he asks whether Ye's many-body clock work belongs in the citation.
responses.response: The overlap concern is the strongest argument against my choice and I answer it with citation wording: the prize is for the magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift and removes Doppler and recoil effects while holding many atoms, not for better clocks in general. That is why my citation names the magic-wavelength trap and the 10^-18 level. On your question about Ye, I would not widen the citation to the whole many-body and Fermi-degenerate programme. I would keep it to the lattice-clock invention and its realization, so that it does not reopen the boundary with the ion-clock community, but I regard that programme as the evidence that Ye's credit is physics and not only performance. Your own concession that the Toner-Tu exponents are only partly confirmed is why I cannot place B006 ahead of a result measured to eighteen digits, and I note that you accept B024 as your first-choice alternative on the merits of its clarity.

responses.point: Kroll discloses a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory, asks whether it requires recusal on the clock discussion, and argues that the committee should state the novelty argument explicitly in the citation and not call the lattice clock a successor to the comb.
responses.response: I take the framing point from Kroll and drop the word successor from my own wording: calling the work a successor to the comb invites the reading incremental. On the disclosure, I think a past research stay in the laboratory of a laureate whose prize forms only the boundary of the argument is a disclosure to be recorded and not a ground for recusal, because Kroll has no documented tie to Katori or Ye and his reasoning on B024 has been the most careful about the comb boundary. As chair I would record it and let the committee confirm that view. I would add that Kroll prefers handling the omitted clock groups in the citation wording and not by enlarging the prize beyond two names, and I agree.

responses.point: Olsson moved from B001 to B024, asks whether Ye is credited for co-invention or for realization, and says the chronology of the first demonstration needs checking before the citation is fixed.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson that this is the main open point for the credit, and I tried to handle it by wording. My citation credits the pair jointly for the invention of the lattice clock and its realization at 10^-18, without assigning separate priority for the proposal. If the chronology showed that Ye's group was only a later demonstrator, I would still keep Ye on the grounds of the record accuracy and many-body physics, and a prize drafted around realization is defensible, but I would say that in the citation. Her test that a tool qualifies when it makes a new class of measurement possible and not only a faster one is the criterion that I apply to B024, and the same test is why I did not carry B001 or B058 into my configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 on the basis of attribution and surprise, says B024 is the best-attributed and most mature candidate, and asks colleagues to say what degree of interpretive maturity they require of B003.
responses.response: My answer to Eriksson's question is that I require the observation and its reproducibility to be secure, not the mechanism, and for the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes at the magic angle that requirement is met. What I additionally need is a credit that can be assigned in three names, and there Eriksson himself says the three-person rule forces the cost of omitting the experimental first author and that earlier twist-angle band work by Lopes dos Santos and others complicates the theory credit. I would keep Bistritzer if B003 were chosen, since the 2011 calculation has two authors. His own statement that he would accept B024 if the moire interpretation is judged too unsettled is the point on which I think the committee can converge, and I would rather vote B024 now than ask B003 to carry an allocation we cannot defend.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's role is best credited as co-invention or as realization to record accuracy; the chronology cannot be verified from the supplied record, so the citation avoids assigning separate priority.
Whether a minority of colleagues will read B024 as a third prize in the comb and ion-clock lineage, and whether the magic-wavelength wording is enough to answer it.
Whether two names fairly capture a field where Lemonde, Sterr, Hollberg, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups contributed decisively.
Whether B003 will prove the stronger choice if the pairing mechanism is clarified and a defensible three-name credit emerges, in which case waiting a few years would favour it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B024, B003 or B023 from my profile: my documented ties are to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur and to KTH astroparticle physics, none of which involves the credited names. I remain in the same broad field as B035 (IceCube), which I do not include in my preferred configuration, and I keep that field proximity flagged as a possible bias. I have no new disclosure. As chair I note Kroll's Hall laboratory stay and Olsson's Japanese university contacts and recommend they be recorded; neither appears to require recusal.
